metadata.title: AMD, MU, SKHY, AVGO: Chip Stocks Ease Overnight After Selloff On New US Chip Restrictions Targeting China

content.text:
AMD, MU, SKHY, AVGO: Chip Stocks Ease Overnight After Selloff On New US Chip Restrictions Targeting China
-
AMD, MU and AVGO fell between 4% and 7.6% in Monday's session as investors took the new technology export curbs as a potential headwind for chip sales.
-
The U.S. is trying to restrict China and other U.S. adversaries from accessing offshore computing power that uses high-end American processors.
-
Intel fell in overnight trading after Nvidia disclosed that it trimmed its stake in the government-backed chipmaker.
Chip stocks eased in post-market hours on Monday after a sharp drop in the regular session triggered by new U.S. chip curbs targeting AI capacity available to Chinese companies.
SK Hynix (SKHY) led the overnight gains, rising 3.6%. Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) and Micron (MU) rose 2% and 2.8% respectively and Broadcom (AVGO) gained 2.3% in what appears to be a relief rally.
AMD, MU and AVGO fell between 4% and 7.6% in Monday's session as investors took the new U.S. technology export curbs as a potential headwind for chip sales. Intel (INTC), which fell 7%, continued to be in the red in overnight trading as Nvidia disclosed it trimmed its stake in the government-backed chipmaker.
US Imposes License On AI Chips Sales To Overseas Data Centers
The Donald Trump administration on Monday moved to limit several countries from providing Chinese companies remote access to advanced AI chips and servers, following increased scrutiny over its handling of curbs on semiconductor exports after an alleged spy scandal involving Nvidia Corp (NVDA).
An interim rule issued by the Commerce Department now requires data center operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil to obtain a license from Washington before exporting advanced AI chips from Nvidia and other U.S. manufacturers to customers in those countries.
The measure is an attempt to restrict China and other U.S. adversaries from accessing offshore computing power that uses high-end American processors.
Nvidia Fallout Revives US-China Tension
The government's directive came days after Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO following his admission to an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International whom the U.S. authorities suspect of being a Chinese spy.
Megaspeed was already under a U.S. investigation for possible export control violations. Nvidia will report third-quarter results on Tuesday and will likely face tough questions about Huang and the chipmaker's dealings with Megaspeed.
